items.stem: A 31-year-old G3P2 woman with a prior hydropic stillbirth from anti-D alloimmunization has an anti-D titer of 1:64 at 22 weeks. Her partner is heterozygous for the D antigen. What is the next step in surveillance?
options: Serial maternal titers every two weeks and delivery planning at 34 weeks
Amniocentesis for bilirubin by optical density at 22 weeks
Intrauterine transfusion at the next visit
Serial middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity measurements
items.explanation: A titer above the critical threshold, usually 1:16 to 1:32, calls for noninvasive fetal anemia surveillance with Doppler of the middle cerebral artery, which replaced amniotic fluid spectrophotometry. Titers alone no longer track severity once critical. Amniocentesis carries a risk of worsening sensitization. Transfusion is reserved for documented anemia, such as a velocity above 1.5 multiples of the median.

items.stem: A 51-year-old woman on tamoxifen for breast cancer has frequent, bothersome hot flashes and declines systemic estrogen. Which nonhormonal agent is most appropriate?
options: Paroxetine
Venlafaxine
Fluoxetine
Bupropion
items.explanation: Venlafaxine reduces vasomotor symptoms with little effect on tamoxifen metabolism. Paroxetine and fluoxetine strongly inhibit CYP2D6, lowering conversion of tamoxifen to endoxifen and possibly reducing its benefit. Bupropion is also a CYP2D6 inhibitor and has no proven value for hot flashes. Systemic estrogen is contraindicated after hormone-receptor positive breast cancer. Gabapentin is another nonhormonal option when an antidepressant is unsuitable.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman with a family history of intellectual disability in a male cousin is found to carry an FMR1 premutation of about 90 CGG repeats. She asks about the associated reproductive risks. Which statement is most accurate?
options: She has increased risk of primary ovarian insufficiency, and the repeat can expand in her offspring
She will have a normal reproductive course and cannot pass the repeat on
She has no personal risk, but all of her daughters will be affected
Her only risk is later-onset dementia, and her children are not at risk
items.explanation: Women with a premutation of 55 to 200 repeats have an increased risk of primary ovarian insufficiency and are at risk of late-onset tremor and ataxia. During maternal transmission the repeat can expand to a full mutation, causing fragile X syndrome in offspring, with risk rising with repeat size. Normal fertility and no transmission is incorrect, and neither inheritance statement is accurate.

items.stem: A 24-year-old pregnant woman at 14 weeks received the first dose of the three-dose human papillomavirus vaccine series two months ago. What is the best advice about the remaining doses?
options: Give the second dose today and the third dose in 4 months
Restart the full series after delivery
Delay the remaining doses until after delivery
Stop the series, since she is now pregnant
items.explanation: The human papillomavirus vaccine is not recommended during pregnancy because safety data are limited, although no adverse outcomes have been linked to inadvertent doses. If pregnancy is discovered mid-series, remaining doses are delayed until after delivery, and the series does not need to be restarted. Vaccination can be given postpartum and during lactation without any special precautions.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman has a recognized dome cystotomy during an abdominal hysterectomy. It is repaired in two layers and the closure is watertight on retrograde filling. What is the most appropriate postoperative bladder management?
options: Continuous catheter drainage for about 7 to 14 days
Catheter removal before she leaves the recovery room
Catheter drainage for 6 weeks, then a cystogram
Bilateral ureteral stents for 6 weeks
items.explanation: A simple dome cystotomy heals well when repaired in two watertight layers, and continuous catheter drainage for about 7 to 14 days keeps the bladder decompressed while the closure seals. A cystogram before removal is added when the injury is complex or near the trigone. Removing the catheter at once risks tension on a fresh suture line, six weeks of drainage is excessive, and ureteral stents address ureteral injury, not bladder injury.

items.stem: A 35-year-old G3P2 at 34 weeks has had pruritus of the palms and soles for two weeks. Serum total bile acids are 108 micromoles per liter. Fetal testing is reassuring and she takes ursodeoxycholic acid. When should delivery be planned?
options: At 37 0/7 weeks
At 39 0/7 weeks
At 40 0/7 weeks unless labor begins
At 36 0/7 weeks
items.explanation: Stillbirth risk in intrahepatic cholestasis rises with bile acid concentration, with a marked increase when levels reach 100 micromoles per liter or higher. For that level, delivery is recommended at 36 0/7 weeks, even with reassuring testing. Lower bile acid levels allow later timing, in the 36 to 39 week range, but continuing to 37, 39 or 40 weeks is unsafe at this level.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman who smokes 20 cigarettes daily requests a highly effective reversible contraceptive. She has no other medical problems. Which method is the best choice?
options: Combined oral contraceptive pill
Levonorgestrel intrauterine system
Transdermal combined estrogen and progestin patch
Vaginal combined ring
items.explanation: Estrogen-containing methods are acceptable at this age because she is under 35, but a heavy smoker should avoid them once she reaches 35, and many experts prefer progestin methods in heavy smokers. The levonorgestrel intrauterine system is highly effective, long acting, and carries no estrogen thrombotic risk. The pill, patch, and ring each deliver estrogen and are less effective in typical use.

items.stem: In a case-control study of congenital anomalies, mothers of affected infants report more medication use in pregnancy than mothers of healthy infants, but the medication records show no difference. Which bias best explains the discrepancy?
options: Lead-time bias
Attrition bias
Recall bias
Berkson bias
items.explanation: Mothers of affected infants search their memories for possible causes and report exposures more completely than control mothers, so self-report differs while objective records do not. This is recall bias, a classic problem of case-control designs. Lead-time bias concerns screening and survival, attrition bias arises from loss to follow-up in cohorts and trials, and Berkson bias comes from hospital-based selection.

items.stem: A 67-year-old woman had a normal cervical cytology result with a negative HPV test on each of her last two screenings, five years apart. She has no history of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or higher. What is the best recommendation about further screening?
options: Continue cytology every 3 years for life
Continue annual cytology with HPV testing
Continue cotesting every 5 years until age 75
Stop screening, because adequate negative testing is documented
items.explanation: Cervical screening may stop at age 65 when prior screening was adequate and negative, defined as two consecutive negative cotests or three consecutive negative cytology results within the past 10 years, the most recent within 5 years, with no history of grade 2 or higher precancer. Women with such a history continue for at least 25 years. Continuing at three-year or annual intervals adds harm without benefit, and extending cotesting to age 75 is not supported.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman has a painful, fluctuant 4 cm swelling of the left posterior labium with fever. She has had one similar episode previously. What is the preferred treatment?
options: Needle aspiration followed by a course of oral antibiotics
Incision and drainage with placement of a Word catheter
Oral antibiotics alone
Immediate complete gland excision
items.explanation: A Bartholin gland abscess is treated by incision and drainage with a Word catheter left for about 4 to 6 weeks to form an epithelialized tract. Aspiration alone recurs frequently. Antibiotics without drainage do not clear an abscess. Complete excision is reserved for recurrence after other therapy, and in women over 40 sampling to exclude carcinoma is considered.

items.stem: A 26-year-old G2P1 at 20 weeks has a reactive treponemal and nontreponemal test. She has no symptoms or examination findings, was never treated, and had a negative test in the first trimester more than a year ago. She is not allergic to penicillin. What is the appropriate treatment?
options: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units intramuscularly once
Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 28 days
Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units intramuscularly weekly for 3 weeks
Azithromycin 2 g orally once
items.explanation: Latent syphilis of unknown or late duration, meaning acquired more than a year ago or with unclear timing, requires three weekly doses of benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units. A single dose treats only early syphilis. Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy, and azithromycin has documented treatment failures and does not reliably treat the fetus or mother.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman has fever of 38.9 C, lower abdominal pain, and cervical motion tenderness. Ultrasonography shows a 6 cm complex right adnexal mass consistent with a tubo-ovarian abscess. She is hemodynamically stable. What is the best initial management?
options: Hospitalization with intravenous cefoxitin and doxycycline
Outpatient intramuscular ceftriaxone with oral doxycycline and metronidazole
Immediate laparotomy with salpingo-oophorectomy
Oral metronidazole for 14 days
items.explanation: A tubo-ovarian abscess is a complicated form of pelvic inflammatory disease treated first with inpatient intravenous antibiotics covering gonococcus, chlamydia, and anaerobes, with drainage if there is no response in 48 to 72 hours. Outpatient therapy is for mild disease only. Surgery is reserved for rupture or failure of medical care. Metronidazole alone lacks adequate spectrum.

items.stem: Following a severe maternal morbidity event on the labor unit, a review team maps the sequence of decisions, handoffs, and system factors without assigning individual blame. Which approach does this describe?
options: Failure mode and effects analysis
Peer review for disciplinary action
Root cause analysis
Randomized controlled trial
items.explanation: Root cause analysis is a retrospective method that examines why an adverse event occurred, focusing on systems and processes rather than individuals. Failure mode and effects analysis is prospective and looks ahead for weaknesses before harm occurs. Peer review for discipline targets individual performance. A randomized trial is a research design, not a quality review.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman with a mother and sister who both had endometrial cancer in their forties has an MLH1 pathogenic variant. What is the most appropriate recommendation?
options: Annual endometrial biopsy from age 30 to 35, or hysterectomy after childbearing
Transvaginal ultrasonography with CA-125 measurement every 5 years until age 50
Colonoscopy every 10 years
No surveillance until symptoms appear
items.explanation: Lynch syndrome carries a high lifetime risk of endometrial and ovarian cancer. Options are annual endometrial biopsy beginning at age 30 to 35 or risk-reducing hysterectomy with salpingo-oophorectomy after childbearing, plus colonoscopy every one to two years. Ultrasonography is unreliable for early disease. Colonoscopy at 10-year intervals is too infrequent. Waiting for symptoms misses preventable cancers. Genetic counseling for relatives should also be offered.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman undergoing laparoscopic salpingectomy under sevoflurane and succinylcholine develops a rapid rise in end-tidal carbon dioxide, masseter rigidity, tachycardia, and a temperature climbing to 39.4 C. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
options: Deepen the volatile anesthetic and give more muscle relaxant
Stop the triggering agents and give dantrolene
Give verapamil to control the tachycardia
Apply ice packs and give acetaminophen only
items.explanation: Malignant hyperthermia is a hypermetabolic crisis triggered by volatile agents and succinylcholine. Treatment is to stop the triggers, ventilate with 100 percent oxygen, give dantrolene promptly, and cool the patient while correcting hyperkalemia and acidosis. Deepening the volatile agent worsens the crisis. Verapamil is avoided because with dantrolene it can cause hyperkalemia and cardiac depression, and cooling and antipyretics alone do not stop the muscle process.

items.stem: A 28-year-old G1P0 woman at 38 weeks in active labor has a temperature of 38.6 C, maternal heart rate of 118, fundal tenderness, and fetal tachycardia. What is the best management?
options: Cefazolin alone, with immediate cesarean delivery regardless of progress
Clindamycin alone, with expedited cesarean
Antipyretics and observation until fever persists
Ampicillin and gentamicin, with vaginal delivery pursued
items.explanation: Intraamniotic infection is treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics, typically ampicillin plus gentamicin, started immediately. The diagnosis alone is not an indication for cesarean, and vaginal delivery is preferred if labor progresses. Single narrow agents miss gram-negative coverage. Observation delays therapy and raises neonatal sepsis and maternal morbidity risk. Antibiotics continue after delivery according to the clinical response.

items.stem: A 32-year-old premenopausal woman has a 4 cm simple unilocular ovarian cyst with thin walls, no septations, and no solid components, found incidentally on ultrasonography. She has no symptoms. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Measurement of serum CA-125 and repeat imaging in 6 weeks
Reassurance with no further imaging
Laparoscopic cystectomy
Oral contraceptives to shrink the cyst
items.explanation: Simple cysts of 5 cm or less in premenopausal women are almost always benign functional cysts and need no follow-up. Tumor markers add little in premenopausal women because CA-125 is often falsely raised, so testing and short-interval imaging are unnecessary. Surgery is for suspicious features or symptoms, and oral contraceptives do not hasten resolution of existing cysts.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman at 10 weeks asks about a single abdominal computed tomography scan she had before knowing she was pregnant, with an estimated fetal dose of 20 mGy. What is the best counseling?
options: The dose exceeds the safe limit for the first trimester, so termination is advised
Malformations are expected at any dose above 10 mGy
The dose is below the 50 mGy threshold, so no excess anomalies are expected
Repeat imaging is needed to verify the dose
items.explanation: Fetal doses below 50 mGy are not associated with an increased risk of anomalies or pregnancy loss, and diagnostic imaging should not be withheld when indicated. Termination is not justified at this dose. Malformations are not inevitable at low doses. Repeat imaging would add radiation and cannot improve an estimate that physicists derive from the scan parameters.

items.stem: A 65-year-old healthy woman with a body mass index of 24 has never been screened for osteoporosis and has no fragility fractures. What is the recommended screening test?
options: Quantitative ultrasonography of the heel alone, repeated every 5 years
Serum calcium and vitamin D levels
Plain radiographs of the spine
Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry of the hip and spine
items.explanation: All women aged 65 and older are screened with dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry, the reference standard for diagnosis. Heel ultrasonography is a limited tool that cannot guide a T-score diagnosis. Serum calcium and vitamin D do not reflect bone density. Plain films detect only advanced loss, after substantial bone mass is gone, and expose the patient to unnecessary radiation.

items.stem: Four days after a laparoscopic hysterectomy that used a 12 mm lateral port, a 44-year-old woman has nausea, vomiting, and a tender, firm bulge at the lateral port site. She is afebrile with stable vital signs. What is the best next step?
options: Computed tomography, with surgical repair if incarcerated bowel is shown
Antiemetics and observation at home for a week
A plain abdominal film, with discharge if gas is present
An abdominal binder with review in two weeks
items.explanation: A tender bulge with vomiting after laparoscopy through a port of 10 mm or larger suggests a port-site hernia with possible Richter or incarcerated bowel, which is a surgical problem. Computed tomography confirms the contents and viability, and incarcerated or strangulated bowel needs prompt operative repair. Watching at home, relying on a plain film, or applying a binder risks bowel ischemia. Fascial closure of larger ports reduces the risk.

items.stem: A 30-year-old G3P2 at 36 weeks has ruptured membranes and a prolapsed umbilical cord, with a cervix 3 cm dilated. She is being moved to the operating room and the surgical team needs several minutes to prepare. What temporizing measure is appropriate?
options: Pushing the cord back into the uterus by hand
Starting oxytocin to speed the cervical dilation
Applying fundal pressure while she is moved
Retrograde bladder filling with saline and clamping the catheter
items.explanation: The goal is to relieve compression of the cord by the presenting part until cesarean birth. Options include manual elevation of the presenting part, knee-chest or steep Trendelenburg position, and filling the bladder with about 500 mL of saline through a catheter, then clamping it. Replacing the cord into the uterus risks further compression, oxytocin increases contractions, and fundal pressure drives the head down onto the cord.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman with Addison disease who takes daily prednisone requests medical abortion at 7 weeks of confirmed intrauterine gestation. Which is the most appropriate recommendation?
options: Give the standard mifepristone and misoprostol regimen with no change
Give misoprostol alone at twice the usual dose
Offer uterine aspiration instead of mifepristone
Delay the procedure until 10 weeks and then use mifepristone
items.explanation: Mifepristone blocks glucocorticoid receptors, so chronic adrenal failure or long-term corticosteroid therapy is a contraindication, as the antagonism can precipitate adrenal crisis. Surgical aspiration is the safe alternative at this gestational age. Giving the standard regimen ignores the contraindication. Doubling misoprostol alone is not an established regimen, and waiting until a later gestational age does not remove the contraindication.

items.stem: A 17-year-old girl has never had a period. She has Tanner stage 5 breast development and normal pubic and axillary hair. Examination shows a short blind vaginal pouch. Karyotype is 46,XX and ovarian function is normal on hormone testing. Which diagnosis best explains these findings?
options: Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome with female external phenotype
Mullerian agenesis (Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome)
Imperforate hymen with hematocolpos
Gonadal dysgenesis with a 45,X karyotype
items.explanation: Failure of mullerian duct development leaves the upper vagina and uterus absent while the ovaries, which arise separately, function normally, so puberty and pubic hair are normal in a 46,XX girl. Androgen insensitivity gives a 46,XY karyotype with sparse pubic hair. An imperforate hymen causes cyclic pain and a bulging membrane, not a blind pouch. Turner syndrome causes streak gonads and absent puberty.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman has premenstrual dysphoric disorder confirmed by two cycles of daily ratings. She wants reliable contraception and prefers to avoid an antidepressant. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
options: A drospirenone combined oral contraceptive in a 24-day active regimen
A cyclic benzodiazepine taken in the luteal phase
A long-acting stimulant medication
Oral progesterone alone in the second half of each cycle
items.explanation: A combined oral contraceptive with drospirenone and ethinyl estradiol in a 24-day active regimen is approved for premenstrual dysphoric disorder and also provides contraception, which suits a patient who declines an antidepressant. Benzodiazepines carry dependence risk with weak evidence, stimulants do not treat the underlying mood disorder, and oral progesterone alone has not shown consistent benefit. Antidepressants remain first-line when she is willing to take one.

items.stem: At the end of a laparoscopic salpingectomy in a 30-year-old woman, blood runs steadily down the cannula of a 5 mm lateral lower quadrant port as it is withdrawn, and an abdominal wall hematoma is expanding. What is the best next step?
options: Apply a pressure dressing and send her to recovery
Raise insufflation pressure to 25 mm Hg to tamponade
Place a full-thickness abdominal wall suture or a Foley balloon at the site
Observe, since lateral port-site bleeding stops by itself
items.explanation: Bleeding along a lateral port suggests injury to the inferior epigastric vessels, which lie lateral to the rectus muscle and can bleed into the abdominal wall. Direct control with a full-thickness suture passed through the abdominal wall around the vessel, or a Foley balloon pulled snug against the peritoneum, stops it. Dressings and observation allow a growing hematoma, and high insufflation pressure compromises ventilation while masking, not stopping, the bleeding.

items.stem: A 31-year-old primipara, three weeks postpartum and breastfeeding, has had fever for 4 days despite antibiotic therapy for mastitis. Examination shows a fluctuant, tender 4 cm mass in the right breast. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Stop breastfeeding and bind the breasts
Ultrasound-guided drainage and continued antibiotics
Continue the same antibiotic and recheck in two weeks
Surgical mastectomy of the affected area
items.explanation: A fluctuant mass with persistent fever despite appropriate antibiotics indicates a breast abscess. Management is drainage, preferably ultrasound-guided needle aspiration or incision and drainage, with antibiotics, and breastfeeding can usually continue. Weaning and binding do not drain the collection, further observation only delays definitive treatment, and mastectomy is far beyond what is required for an abscess.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with severe lower abdominal pain, blood pressure of 78/40 mm Hg, and heart rate of 134. Urine hCG is positive, and a focused abdominal scan reveals fluid in Morison pouch. What is the next step?
options: Methotrexate single dose
Repeat quantitative hCG in 48 hours
Transvaginal ultrasonography to locate the pregnancy
Emergency surgery after rapid resuscitation
items.explanation: Hemodynamic instability with hemoperitoneum in a pregnant patient indicates ruptured ectopic pregnancy and requires immediate operative control of bleeding along with resuscitation and blood products. Methotrexate is only for stable patients. Serial hCG and further imaging delay life-saving intervention and are acceptable only in a stable woman with a pregnancy of unknown location. Blood should be crossmatched while the team moves to the operating room.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman with chronic hypertension takes lisinopril and learns at 9 weeks that she is pregnant. She asks why her physician wants to change the medication now when the first trimester is nearly over. Which fetal risk most strongly supports stopping this drug?
options: Fetal renal hypoperfusion causing oligohydramnios and pulmonary hypoplasia
Closure defects of the neural tube from first-trimester exposure
Ebstein anomaly of the tricuspid valve from impaired early cardiac valve formation
Premature constriction of the ductus arteriosus near term
items.explanation: Drugs that block the renin-angiotensin system impair fetal renal perfusion in the second and third trimesters, producing anuria, oligohydramnios, pulmonary hypoplasia, and neonatal renal failure, so they are replaced with an agent such as labetalol. Neural tube defects and Ebstein anomaly are not their classic effects, and ductal constriction is the characteristic effect of nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman at 9 weeks of gestation presents 20 hours after a sexual assault. Which prophylaxis regimen is recommended?
options: Ceftriaxone, doxycycline, and metronidazole for 7 days
Doxycycline alone for 7 days
Observation with testing in two weeks
Ceftriaxone, azithromycin, and metronidazole
items.explanation: Presumptive treatment after assault for a nonpregnant patient is ceftriaxone, doxycycline, and metronidazole, but doxycycline is avoided in pregnancy, so a single dose of azithromycin replaces it and metronidazole is kept for trichomoniasis. Postexposure prophylaxis against HIV within 72 hours and hepatitis B vaccination if not immune are also offered. Doxycycline alone leaves gonorrhea untreated, and waiting delays time-sensitive protection.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman with ovarian cancer will undergo an abdominal hysterectomy with debulking expected to last 4 hours. She has a body mass index of 31 and no prior thromboembolism. Which is the best prophylaxis against venous thromboembolism?
options: Pneumatic compression plus anticoagulation continued after discharge
Early ambulation alone
Graduated compression stockings alone, started at induction of anesthesia
Aspirin 81 mg daily
items.explanation: Major abdominopelvic surgery for cancer in an older patient places her in a high-risk category, for which combined mechanical and pharmacologic prophylaxis is advised, and for cancer surgery extended prophylaxis for up to four weeks after surgery lowers events. Ambulation or stockings alone are suitable only for low-risk operations, and aspirin is not an accepted substitute for anticoagulant prophylaxis.

items.stem: A 33-year-old G3P2 woman with two prior cesarean deliveries has a positive pregnancy test at 7 weeks. Ultrasonography shows a gestational sac embedded in the anterior lower uterine segment at the scar, with an empty cavity. What is the recommended approach?
options: Manage expectantly to viability with serial ultrasonography every 2 weeks
Terminate the pregnancy with methotrexate or ultrasound-guided evacuation
Perform blind dilation and sharp curettage
Give misoprostol alone for expulsion
items.explanation: A cesarean scar pregnancy risks uterine rupture and hemorrhage and may progress to placenta accreta spectrum, so early termination is advised using methotrexate, ultrasound-guided suction, or a combination. Expectant management carries a high risk of serious morbidity. Blind sharp curettage can precipitate catastrophic bleeding, and misoprostol alone seldom resolves an implanted scar gestation. Follow-up with hCG and ultrasonography confirms resolution.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman is followed after suction evacuation of a complete hydatidiform mole. Her hCG values on four consecutive weekly measurements are 4,100, 4,000, 4,200, and 4,050 mIU/mL. What is the correct interpretation?
options: Normal regression of hCG, so continue weekly monitoring without staging
Retained products, which require repeat curettage only
Plateau, consistent with gestational trophoblastic neoplasia
A new intrauterine pregnancy
items.explanation: A plateau, defined as a change of 10 percent or less over four values across three weeks, meets criteria for postmolar gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, prompting staging and chemotherapy. Normal regression shows a steady fall. Repeat curettage is not routine unless bleeding or retained tissue is documented. A new pregnancy would show a rising value, and effective contraception is advised during follow-up.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman at 36 weeks, who has decision-making capacity, declines a recommended cesarean birth for a persistent transverse lie after a full discussion of the risks. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Respect her refusal, continue counseling, and document informed refusal
Obtain a court order to perform the cesarean
Ask her partner to consent on her behalf
Perform the cesarean once labor begins under an emergency exception
items.explanation: A pregnant woman with decision-making capacity has the right to refuse any treatment, including surgery recommended for fetal benefit, even when the clinician disagrees. The physician continues to counsel, addresses her concerns, offers alternatives, and documents the informed refusal. Court orders and surrogate consent override her autonomy and are not supported by professional ethics guidance, and operating under an emergency exception after she has refused would be battery.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman who smokes 15 cigarettes daily wants to quit and has failed nicotine patches alone. She has no psychiatric history. Which addition is most effective?
options: Naltrexone
Clonidine alone
Varenicline
Modafinil
items.explanation: Varenicline, a partial nicotinic agonist, is among the most effective single agents for cessation and can be combined with counseling or nicotine replacement. Naltrexone is used for opioid dependence. Clonidine has limited evidence. Modafinil has not been shown to improve quit rates. Combination nicotine replacement is another strong option. Large trials found no excess neuropsychiatric harm.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman in labor with ruptured membranes for 14 hours requires cesarean birth for arrest of descent. In addition to cefazolin, which measure reduces postoperative endometritis?
options: Delaying the antibiotic dose until after cord clamping
Routine continuation of antibiotics for five days afterward
Omitting the urinary catheter during surgery
Vaginal cleansing with povidone-iodine before surgery
items.explanation: In women in labor or with ruptured membranes, cleansing the vagina with povidone-iodine solution immediately before cesarean lowers the risk of postoperative endometritis, in addition to prophylactic antibiotic timed before the incision. Delaying antibiotic until cord clamping is no longer advised, because the earlier dose reduces infection without harming the newborn. Extended antibiotic courses add nothing, and omitting a catheter does not address infection.

items.stem: A 30-year-old G2P1 woman with HIV is at 36 weeks with a viral load of 1,800 copies per mL despite adherence to antiretroviral therapy. What is the best plan for delivery?
options: Vaginal delivery at term with intravenous zidovudine only if labor starts
Scheduled cesarean at 38 weeks with intravenous zidovudine
Induction at 41 weeks with oral therapy only
Cesarean after labor begins, without zidovudine
items.explanation: A viral load above 1,000 copies per mL near delivery is an indication for scheduled cesarean at 38 weeks, with intravenous zidovudine started 3 hours before surgery, to reduce vertical transmission. Vaginal delivery is appropriate only when viral load is 1,000 or lower. Waiting until 41 weeks or until labor starts removes the benefit of an elective cesarean before membranes rupture.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman at 22 weeks is diagnosed with invasive ductal breast carcinoma that requires anthracycline-based chemotherapy. What is the correct counseling about timing?
options: Chemotherapy must wait until after delivery
Chemotherapy is considered safe only if started during the first trimester of pregnancy
Chemotherapy can begin now and should stop about 3 weeks before delivery
Chemotherapy should continue until the day of delivery
items.explanation: After organogenesis, chemotherapy in the second and third trimesters carries a low risk of major malformation, so treatment need not be delayed. It should end about three weeks before expected delivery to allow recovery of maternal and neonatal blood counts. The first trimester is the period of greatest teratogenic risk. Waiting for delivery harms maternal outcome, and treating through delivery risks neutropenia and sepsis.

items.stem: Investigators want to learn whether a rare congenital uterine anomaly is associated with a maternal exposure. They compare the exposure histories of 40 affected girls with those of 160 unaffected girls. Which study design is this?
options: Cohort study
Randomized controlled trial
Cross-sectional survey
Case-control study
items.explanation: A case-control study starts with the outcome, selecting affected and unaffected people and looking back at exposure, which makes it efficient for rare conditions, and its measure of association is the odds ratio. A cohort study follows exposed and unexposed people forward and suits common outcomes. A randomized trial assigns the exposure, which is not possible here, and a cross-sectional survey measures exposure and outcome at one time without selecting by outcome.

items.stem: A 23-year-old woman has dysuria and purulent cervical discharge. Nucleic acid amplification testing is positive for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and negative for chlamydia. She has no drug allergies. Which is the recommended treatment?
options: Ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly once
Azithromycin 1 g orally once
Ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally once
Penicillin G benzathine intramuscularly once
items.explanation: Uncomplicated gonorrhea is treated with a single intramuscular dose of ceftriaxone, 500 mg for persons under 150 kg, because resistance has eliminated fluoroquinolones and made azithromycin monotherapy unreliable. Doxycycline is added only when chlamydia has not been excluded, which it has here. Partners are treated and the patient is retested in three months. Benzathine penicillin is the treatment for syphilis, not gonorrhea, and does not reliably clear this organism.

items.stem: Seven days after a total abdominal hysterectomy, a 50-year-old woman has a fever of 38.9 C, pelvic pain, and leukocytosis. Computed tomography shows a 6 cm rim-enhancing collection at the vaginal cuff. She is hemodynamically stable. What is the best management?
options: Oral antibiotics alone with review in one week
Broad-spectrum antibiotics with image-guided drainage
Immediate laparotomy for abscess removal
Observation, because the collection will reabsorb
items.explanation: A rim-enhancing pelvic collection with fever after hysterectomy is a cuff or pelvic abscess. Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics covering gram-negative organisms and anaerobes are combined with percutaneous or transvaginal image-guided drainage for a collection of this size. Oral antibiotics alone rarely clear an abscess, laparotomy is reserved for failed drainage or instability, and observation risks sepsis.

items.stem: Immediately after delivery of the placenta in a 27-year-old G3P2 woman, a smooth, round mass is seen at the introitus and she becomes hypotensive and bradycardic. What is the first step?
options: Replace the uterus manually without delay
Administer oxytocin to contract the uterus
Remove the placenta if it remains attached
Wait for spontaneous reduction
items.explanation: Uterine inversion causes neurogenic shock and hemorrhage and requires immediate manual replacement before the cervical ring tightens. Uterotonics should be withheld, and tocolytic agents may be used if needed, until the uterus is replaced. A still-attached placenta is left in place until after replacement to limit bleeding. Waiting allows progressive edema, shock, and increased mortality. Uterine relaxants such as nitroglycerin can assist replacement if the ring is tight.

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman has found a 2 cm smooth, mobile, painless breast mass on self-examination. She has no family history of cancer. What is the best initial imaging?
options: Screening mammography
Breast magnetic resonance imaging
Breast ultrasonography
Positron emission tomography
items.explanation: In women younger than 30, dense breast tissue limits mammography and ultrasonography is the preferred first test to separate solid from cystic masses. Mammography exposes young breasts to radiation with low yield. Magnetic resonance imaging is reserved for high-risk screening or problem solving. Positron emission tomography has no role in the initial assessment of a palpable mass.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman has taken daily tenofovir with emtricitabine for preexposure prophylaxis for three months because her partner is HIV positive. She is adherent and well. Which monitoring is recommended at this visit?
options: CD4 count and HIV viral load
Hepatitis C RNA and a bone density scan
No testing until the six-month visit
Repeat HIV antigen and antibody testing, with sexually transmitted infection screening
items.explanation: Preexposure prophylaxis requires HIV testing at least every 3 months, because continuing the drug during an unrecognized infection risks resistance, along with screening for sexually transmitted infections and a review of adherence and risk. Creatinine clearance is checked less often, usually every 6 to 12 months. CD4 counts and viral loads belong to the care of people with HIV, and routine bone density scans are not part of monitoring.

items.stem: Four days after an abdominal hysterectomy for a large fibroid uterus, a 49-year-old woman has left flank pain, fever of 38.4 C, and clear fluid leaking from the vagina. Creatinine is slightly higher than baseline. What is the best next diagnostic step?
options: Plain abdominal radiograph
CT urogram with delayed excretory images
Repeat pelvic examination in 48 hours
Colonoscopy
items.explanation: Flank pain, fever, and watery vaginal leakage after hysterectomy suggest ureteral injury with a ureterovaginal fistula or urinoma, and a CT urogram with delayed images shows the site of extravasation or obstruction. Treatment is stent placement or percutaneous nephrostomy, with repair if needed. A plain film and waiting do not show the leak, and colonoscopy evaluates the bowel, not the urinary tract.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman on postoperative day 2 after a cesarean delivery for arrest of labor has a temperature of 38.7 C, uterine tenderness, and foul lochia. Her wound is clean. Which regimen is appropriate?
options: Oral amoxicillin for 5 days
Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin
Clindamycin plus gentamicin
Vancomycin alone
items.explanation: Postpartum endometritis is polymicrobial, and clindamycin with gentamicin is the standard first-line regimen, covering anaerobes and gram-negative organisms, continued until the patient is afebrile for 24 hours. Oral amoxicillin is inadequate for a systemic infection. Ceftriaxone with azithromycin targets sexually transmitted organisms. Vancomycin alone misses gram-negative bacteria and anaerobes, so it is reserved for resistant gram-positive infection.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman reports spontaneous bloody discharge from one duct of the left nipple. Examination shows no palpable mass. What is the best next step?
options: Reassurance and continued annual screening mammography
Bilateral breast reduction
Empiric antibiotics for ductitis
Diagnostic mammography and ultrasonography
items.explanation: Spontaneous unilateral discharge from one duct that is bloody or clear raises concern for intraductal papilloma or malignancy and needs diagnostic imaging, followed by surgical duct excision if no cause is found. Reassurance would miss malignancy. Reduction surgery is not diagnostic. Antibiotics treat periductal infection, which presents with pain, erythema, and purulent rather than bloody discharge.

items.stem: A 26-year-old transgender man has taken testosterone for two years and has had amenorrhea since the first year. He has vaginal intercourse with a male partner and asks whether testosterone prevents pregnancy. What is the best counseling?
options: Testosterone is not contraception, so offer an effective method
Amenorrhea on testosterone makes pregnancy impossible
Testosterone must stop first for any method to work
Only a combined estrogen pill is acceptable
items.explanation: Testosterone does not reliably suppress ovulation, and pregnancy can occur despite amenorrhea, while testosterone is teratogenic and should not be used in pregnancy. He should be offered effective contraception, such as an intrauterine device, implant, or progestin-only method, chosen with his preferences and any dysphoria in mind. Amenorrhea is not protection, stopping testosterone is unnecessary, and estrogen-containing methods are generally unwelcome and not required.

items.stem: Three days after a cesarean through a Pfannenstiel incision, a 30-year-old woman has sharp burning pain in the suprapubic area that radiates to the labia and medial upper thigh. Pain is worse on standing straight and relieved by hip flexion. There is no motor weakness. Which nerve is most likely involved?
options: Femoral nerve branch
Ilioinguinal nerve
Obturator nerve branch
Pudendal nerve branches
items.explanation: Ilioinguinal and iliohypogastric nerves can be trapped or cut at the lateral edge of a low transverse incision, causing burning pain over the suprapubic skin and the anterior labia and medial thigh, relieved by hip flexion that relaxes tension. Femoral injury causes knee extension weakness, obturator injury causes weak adduction, and pudendal nerve involvement causes perineal pain.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman at 20 weeks has a normal platelet count. Her previous newborn had a platelet count of 8,000 per microliter and died of intracranial hemorrhage, with anti-HPA-1a antibodies confirmed, and the father is homozygous for HPA-1a. What is the most appropriate maternal therapy?
options: Intravenous immune globulin, with or without prednisone
Weekly platelet transfusions given to the mother until delivery
Anti-D immune globulin
Maternal plasmapheresis alone
items.explanation: Fetal and neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia arises when maternal antibodies cross the placenta and destroy fetal platelets. Weekly maternal intravenous immune globulin, with or without steroids, is the standard noninvasive therapy. Maternal platelet counts are normal in this condition, so maternal transfusion is irrelevant. Anti-D acts on red cell alloimmunization. Plasmapheresis is not first-line. Fetal blood sampling is avoided because of bleeding risk.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman has thin gray vaginal discharge with a fishy odor. Vaginal pH is 5.2, clue cells are seen on saline microscopy, and the amine test is positive. What is the recommended treatment?
options: Fluconazole 150 mg orally once
Metronidazole 500 mg orally twice daily for 7 days
Azithromycin 1 g orally once
Ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly once
items.explanation: The patient meets Amsel criteria for bacterial vaginosis, treated with oral metronidazole for 7 days, or with intravaginal metronidazole or clindamycin. Fluconazole treats candidiasis, which presents with thick discharge, normal pH, and hyphae. Treating asymptomatic partners is not recommended, and recurrence is common. Azithromycin and ceftriaxone treat chlamydia and gonorrhea, which are not demonstrated by these findings.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman took ulipristal acetate for emergency contraception today. She wants to start combined oral contraceptive pills for ongoing contraception. What is the correct advice?
options: Start the pills today for added protection against pregnancy
Start the pills tomorrow without any other precautions
Wait 5 days to start the pills and use a barrier method meanwhile
Avoid every hormonal method for the next 3 months
items.explanation: Ulipristal is a selective progesterone receptor modulator, and starting a progestin-containing method immediately may reduce its effect. Guidance is to wait 5 days before starting hormonal contraception and to use condoms or abstain during that time. Starting today or tomorrow could blunt ulipristal's delay of ovulation, while a three-month wait is unnecessary and leaves her unprotected longer.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman with epilepsy on valproate becomes pregnant unplanned at 6 weeks and has been seizure-free for two years. What is the best advice?
options: Stop all antiseizure medication immediately until the first trimester ends
Continue valproate at a higher dose
Switch to phenytoin at once
Switch to lamotrigine if feasible, and take folic acid daily
items.explanation: Valproate carries the highest risk of neural tube defects and neurodevelopmental effects, so transition to a safer drug such as lamotrigine or levetiracetam is advised, ideally with levels monitored. Abrupt withdrawal risks seizures that endanger mother and fetus. Raising the valproate dose increases exposure. Phenytoin is also teratogenic and is not a preferred substitute. Lamotrigine clearance rises in pregnancy, so levels guide dose changes.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman has used clobetasol ointment for lichen sclerosus for four months with good symptom control. A 1.5 cm firm, white, thickened, ulcerated area persists on the left labium minus. What is the best next step?
options: Increasing clobetasol to twice daily for three more months
Adding oral fluconazole for presumed candidiasis
Biopsy of the lesion
Switching to topical estradiol cream for atrophy
items.explanation: A thickened, ulcerated, or raised area that persists in lichen sclerosus despite adequate treatment must be biopsied, because differentiated vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia and squamous cell carcinoma arise in this skin. Intensifying the same steroid delays the diagnosis. Fluconazole addresses candidiasis, which does not explain a firm ulcerated lesion, and estradiol treats atrophy but not a suspicious focus. Lifelong surveillance of lichen sclerosus is advised for this reason.

items.stem: A 30-year-old nonpregnant woman has reactive treponemal and nontreponemal tests, no symptoms, no prior treatment, and no history that dates her infection. Examination is normal. Which treatment is recommended?
options: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units intramuscularly once
Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days
Ceftriaxone 1 g daily for 3 days
Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units intramuscularly weekly for 3 weeks
items.explanation: Latent syphilis of unknown duration is treated as late latent disease with benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units intramuscularly once weekly for three weeks, because the single dose used for early syphilis is not enough. Doxycycline for 7 days and a short ceftriaxone course are not adequate substitutes. Titers are followed after therapy to confirm a fourfold decline, and partners are evaluated and treated as indicated.

items.stem: Twelve hours after cesarean delivery under spinal anesthesia, a 31-year-old woman has a severe positional headache that worsens on standing and eases when lying flat. What is the definitive treatment if conservative measures fail?
options: Epidural saline bolus
Epidural blood patch
Lumbar puncture drainage
Intravenous antibiotics
items.explanation: Postdural puncture headache results from cerebrospinal fluid leak and is positional. Conservative care includes fluids, caffeine, and analgesics, and an epidural blood patch is definitive when these fail. A saline bolus gives only temporary relief. Further lumbar puncture would worsen the leak. Antibiotics are used for meningitis, which presents with fever and neck stiffness. Symptoms usually appear within five days of the puncture.

items.stem: A 13-year-old girl has had cyclic lower abdominal pain for four months and has not had menarche despite breast Tanner stage 4. Examination shows a bluish, bulging membrane at the introitus. What is the next step?
options: Surgical incision of the hymen
Observation until spontaneous opening
Combined oral contraceptive pills to suppress cycles
Laparoscopic hysterectomy
items.explanation: Imperforate hymen traps menstrual blood and causes hematocolpos with cyclic pain and primary amenorrhea. The treatment is simple hymenotomy, usually with excellent outcomes. Waiting risks hematometra and endometriosis from retrograde flow. Suppression of cycles does not relieve the obstruction. Hysterectomy is not indicated because the uterus and vagina are normal. Ultrasonography confirms the diagnosis if the membrane is not obvious.

items.stem: A 16-year-old girl has painful periods that cause her to miss school for one to two days each month. Her pelvic examination is normal and she is not sexually active. She has taken acetaminophen without relief. Which is the best next step?
options: Perform diagnostic laparoscopy
Start a nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drug at the onset of menses
Begin a gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist for six months of therapy
Refer for hysteroscopy to look for adhesions
items.explanation: Primary dysmenorrhea results from prostaglandin release, so nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs started at the first sign of bleeding or pain and continued for two to three days are first-line therapy, with hormonal contraception added if pain persists or contraception is desired. Laparoscopy is considered for refractory pain to look for endometriosis, and a GnRH agonist or hysteroscopy has no role at the outset.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman has sudden dyspnea, hypotension, and cyanosis, followed by seizure and disseminated intravascular coagulation, during induction of labor at 39 weeks. What is the cornerstone of management?
options: High-dose corticosteroids and antihistamines as definitive treatment
Emergency thoracotomy
Tocolysis to stop contractions
Immediate supportive resuscitation with early delivery planning
items.explanation: Amniotic fluid embolism is a clinical diagnosis with no specific therapy, so care is aggressive supportive resuscitation: oxygenation, vasopressors, blood products for coagulopathy, and delivery when arrest or severe compromise occurs. Steroids have no proven benefit. Thoracotomy has no role. Tocolysis does not help and may worsen hemorrhage afterward. Early involvement of anesthesia, critical care, and the blood bank improves outcome.

items.stem: A 4-year-old girl has had vulvar irritation and a thin membrane that appears to fuse the labia minora, leaving a small anterior opening. She voids normally. What is the best treatment?
options: Manual separation in the clinic
Surgical division under anesthesia
Topical estrogen cream applied to the adhesion
Oral antibiotics for 10 days
items.explanation: Labial adhesions are common in hypoestrogenic prepubertal girls and respond to a short course of topical estrogen cream in most cases. Forceful separation is painful and traumatic and the adhesions often recur. Surgery is reserved for urinary obstruction that fails medical therapy. Antibiotics do not treat a hypoestrogenic adhesion. Parents should be told that recurrence is common but usually mild.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman whose partner has human immunodeficiency virus infection asks about preexposure prophylaxis. Her infection test is negative and her renal function is normal. Which regimen is preferred for protection after vaginal exposure?
options: Daily emtricitabine with tenofovir disoproxil
Daily oral emtricitabine with tenofovir alafenamide
Doxycycline taken after each sexual exposure
Condoms alone with no preventive medication
items.explanation: Daily oral emtricitabine with tenofovir disoproxil fumarate protects after vaginal and rectal exposure and is the preferred oral regimen for women. The alafenamide combination was not studied for receptive vaginal sex and is not preferred. Doxycycline after sex is meant to prevent bacterial infection, not human immunodeficiency virus, and is not recommended for cisgender women. Condoms alone leave her unprotected when they fail. Before starting, infection status is confirmed negative and hepatitis B is screened.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman at 31 weeks has an estimated fetal weight below the third percentile with absent end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery, and the biophysical profile is normal. What is the recommended timing of delivery?
options: Delivery at 37 weeks with continued twice-weekly testing until then
Delivery at 39 weeks
Delivery at about 32 weeks with antenatal corticosteroids
Delivery immediately without steroids
items.explanation: Fetal growth restriction with absent end-diastolic flow warrants delivery around 32 weeks if testing stays reassuring, and earlier if testing deteriorates, with corticosteroids and magnesium as indicated. Waiting to 37 or 39 weeks suits only isolated growth restriction with normal Doppler. Immediate delivery without steroids ignores their benefit when time permits. Doppler findings, not size alone, set the schedule.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman has frothy yellow-green discharge, vulvar itching, and a strawberry-appearing cervix. Wet mount shows motile flagellated organisms. Which plan is correct?
options: Metronidazole for 7 days, partner treatment, and retesting in 3 months
Single-dose metronidazole 2 g, with partner treatment deferred until symptoms
Clotrimazole cream, with retesting at 6 weeks
Doxycycline for 7 days, with no retesting
items.explanation: Women with trichomoniasis receive oral metronidazole 500 mg twice daily for 7 days, which outperforms the single dose, and sexual partners are treated at the same time. Retesting is advised at three months because reinfection is common. Partners should avoid intercourse until both have finished treatment. Antifungal cream treats candidiasis. Doxycycline is not an effective therapy for this protozoan infection.

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman 6 days after a vaginal delivery is brought in by her partner because she believes the baby is possessed, sleeps little, and has hallucinations. She has no history of mental illness. What is the best management?
options: Outpatient sertraline and psychotherapy, with a follow-up visit in 2 weeks
Reassurance, as this is postpartum blues
Cognitive behavioral therapy only
Emergency psychiatric admission with antipsychotic therapy
items.explanation: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency with a risk of suicide and infanticide, usually starting within two weeks of delivery. Hospitalization with antipsychotic or mood-stabilizing therapy is required, and the infant must be supervised. Postpartum blues are brief and lack psychosis. Antidepressant monotherapy can worsen bipolar illness. Therapy alone is inadequate for acute psychosis. Lactation decisions are individualized.

items.stem: A 22-year-old woman has cycles every 45 to 90 days, acne, and hirsutism. She has an elevated free testosterone and a normal prolactin and TSH. She does not desire pregnancy. Which is the best initial treatment?
options: Clomiphene citrate
A combined hormonal contraceptive
Cyclic bromocriptine
Gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist
items.explanation: Irregular ovulation with clinical hyperandrogenism after excluding thyroid disease and hyperprolactinemia meets criteria for polycystic ovary syndrome. A combined hormonal contraceptive regulates bleeding, lowers androgen production, increases sex hormone binding globulin, and protects the endometrium. Clomiphene treats infertility, not symptoms in a woman not seeking pregnancy, bromocriptine treats hyperprolactinemia, and a GnRH agonist is not indicated.

items.stem: A 22-year-old G1P0 woman at 9 weeks has had persistent vomiting for three weeks, has lost 6 kg, and is confused with horizontal nystagmus. What should be given first?
options: Intravenous dextrose and normal saline before giving any vitamins
Oral ondansetron and discharge
Oral doxylamine and pyridoxine at home
Intravenous thiamine before any glucose-containing fluid
items.explanation: Hyperemesis gravidarum with confusion and nystagmus suggests Wernicke encephalopathy, caused by thiamine deficiency. Thiamine must precede dextrose, which can precipitate or worsen the syndrome. Giving glucose first risks irreversible neurologic injury. Replacement continues for several days, along with correction of electrolytes. Oral antiemetics and outpatient doxylamine with pyridoxine are appropriate for mild nausea but cannot treat this emergency.

items.stem: A 51-year-old woman with an intact uterus has had no period for 14 months and has daily severe hot flashes that disrupt sleep. She has no history of breast cancer, thromboembolism, or liver disease. Her blood pressure is normal. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Systemic estrogen combined with a progestogen
Systemic estrogen alone
Vaginal estrogen cream only
Daily soy isoflavone supplements
items.explanation: Systemic estrogen is the most effective treatment for bothersome vasomotor symptoms, and in a woman within ten years of menopause and without contraindications the benefits outweigh risks. Because her uterus is present, a progestogen must be added to prevent endometrial hyperplasia. Unopposed estrogen would raise cancer risk, low-dose vaginal estrogen treats genitourinary symptoms and does not relieve hot flashes, and soy has no reliable effect.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman at 39 weeks in labor has a positive group B streptococcus culture and a history of a nonsevere rash with penicillin. Isolate susceptibility is unknown. Which intrapartum antibiotic is recommended?
options: Clindamycin
Cefazolin
Gentamicin
Azithromycin
items.explanation: For patients at low risk of anaphylaxis, cefazolin is the recommended alternative to penicillin for group B streptococcus prophylaxis. Clindamycin is used only when the isolate is shown to be susceptible, and it is not appropriate when susceptibility is unknown. Gentamicin lacks adequate activity as a single agent. Azithromycin is not recommended for this indication.

items.stem: A 34-year-old nulligravid woman has heavy menstrual bleeding and infertility for two years. Hysteroscopy shows a 2 cm submucosal fibroid that is mostly intracavitary. She wants to conceive. Which is the best treatment?
options: Uterine artery embolization
Total abdominal hysterectomy
Hysteroscopic myomectomy
Long-term gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist
items.explanation: A submucosal fibroid distorting the cavity can cause bleeding and impair implantation, and hysteroscopic resection removes it while preserving the uterus and improving fertility prospects. Embolization is generally avoided in women who wish to conceive because of possible effects on ovarian and endometrial blood supply. Hysterectomy ends fertility, and a GnRH agonist shrinks fibroids only temporarily and does not allow conception.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman who is varicella nonimmune develops a vesicular rash with fever the day after a vaginal birth at term. Her newborn is healthy and has no rash. What is the best management for the newborn?
options: Give varicella zoster immune globulin to the newborn
Give oral acyclovir to the newborn only
Observe the newborn with no treatment
Give the live varicella vaccine to the newborn
items.explanation: Maternal varicella that begins from 5 days before to 2 days after delivery is dangerous for the newborn, who has had little time to receive protective maternal antibody, so passive immunization with varicella zoster immune globulin is recommended, with close observation and acyclovir if disease appears. Observation alone is inadequate, and the live vaccine is not given to newborns for exposure prophylaxis.

items.stem: A 22-year-old college student presents with a low-grade fever, lower abdominal pain, and uterine and adnexal tenderness with cervical motion tenderness. She is not pregnant, has no abscess on ultrasonography, tolerates oral intake, and can return for follow-up. What is the best management?
options: Azithromycin 1 g orally once
Ceftriaxone intramuscularly once with no further drugs
Doxycycline alone for 7 days
Ceftriaxone intramuscularly once, with doxycycline and metronidazole for 14 days
items.explanation: Mild to moderate pelvic inflammatory disease is treated as an outpatient with ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly once plus doxycycline and metronidazole twice daily for 14 days, covering gonococcus, chlamydia, and anaerobes. Treatment does not wait for test results because delay raises the risk of tubal scarring. Single agents or short courses leave organisms untreated. Admission is for pregnancy, abscess, severe illness, or failure of oral therapy.

items.stem: A 26-year-old Rh(D)-negative woman at 12 weeks undergoes chorionic villus sampling. Her antibody screen is negative and the father of the baby is Rh(D) positive. Which is the best management?
options: Withhold anti-D because the antibody screen is negative
Give anti-D immune globulin within 72 hours of the procedure
Give anti-D only if a Kleihauer-Betke test shows fetomaternal hemorrhage
Delay anti-D until the routine dose at 28 weeks
items.explanation: Invasive prenatal procedures can cause fetomaternal hemorrhage, so an unsensitized Rh-negative woman receives anti-D immune globulin within 72 hours. A negative antibody screen means she is not yet sensitized, which is exactly why prophylaxis works. Quantitative testing is used after delivery or large bleeds to adjust dosing, not to decide after a procedure, and waiting until 28 weeks leaves the exposure unprotected.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis. Vaginal culture grows Candida glabrata, and she failed repeated courses of fluconazole. She is not pregnant. Which treatment is most appropriate?
options: Weekly oral fluconazole maintenance for six months
A longer course of oral fluconazole at higher dose
Intravaginal boric acid capsules nightly for 14 days
Intravaginal metronidazole gel nightly for 5 days
items.explanation: Non-albicans species such as Candida glabrata are often resistant to fluconazole and other azoles. Boric acid 600 mg vaginal capsules nightly for 14 days is the recommended option for these infections. Azole maintenance therapy fails because of resistance, and metronidazole treats bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis, not yeast. Boric acid is toxic if swallowed and is not used in pregnancy.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman at 37 weeks has an isolated finding of an amniotic fluid index of 4 cm. Fetal growth is normal, the nonstress test is reactive, membranes are intact, and she has no other complications. Which is the best plan?
options: Repeat the amniotic fluid index in two weeks
Recommend oral hydration and recheck in one week
Perform amnioinfusion to restore the fluid volume
Offer delivery at this gestational age
items.explanation: Isolated oligohydramnios with intact membranes is generally managed with delivery between 36 0/7 and 37 6/7 weeks, because the risk of stillbirth and cord compression rises with expectant care. At 37 weeks, waiting two weeks or one week passes the recommended window. Maternal hydration may transiently raise the index but does not change outcome, and amnioinfusion is an intrapartum or experimental measure.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman has a complete hydatidiform mole evacuated by suction curettage. Which follow-up plan is most appropriate?
options: Weekly hCG until normal for three weeks, then monthly for three months
A single hCG at 6 weeks, then no further testing and no contraception requirement
Monthly hCG for one month and an early attempt at pregnancy
Hysterectomy planned to prevent malignant progression
items.explanation: After molar evacuation, serial quantitative hCG is checked weekly until undetectable for three consecutive weeks, then monthly for three months, to detect persistent gestational trophoblastic neoplasia. Reliable contraception is advised throughout so that a rising hCG is not confused with a new pregnancy. A single value is inadequate, early conception obscures surveillance, and hysterectomy is not routine for a woman who wants to preserve fertility.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman had gestational diabetes controlled with diet and delivered a healthy infant 5 weeks ago. She is breastfeeding and asks whether she needs any further testing. Which is the best recommendation?
options: Hemoglobin A1c alone at the postpartum visit because it requires no fasting
A random glucose at the next annual visit
A 75 g oral glucose tolerance test between 4 and 12 weeks after delivery
No testing while she continues to breastfeed
items.explanation: Women with gestational diabetes carry a high lifetime risk of type 2 diabetes and should have a 2-hour 75 g glucose tolerance test 4 to 12 weeks after birth, then lifelong screening every one to three years. Hemoglobin A1c is less reliable early after delivery because of blood loss and red cell turnover. A random glucose is insensitive, and breastfeeding does not remove the need for testing.

items.stem: A 78-year-old woman who is not sexually active has symptomatic stage 4 uterovaginal prolapse after a failed pessary trial. She is healthy enough for surgery and wants the lowest chance of recurrence with a short operation. Which procedure is best?
options: Sacrocolpopexy with synthetic mesh
Colpocleisis
Anterior colporrhaphy alone
Pelvic floor muscle training with a new pessary
items.explanation: Colpocleisis closes the vaginal canal and has the lowest recurrence rate, with a short operative time and low morbidity, so it suits an older woman who will not have vaginal intercourse and accepts the permanent change. Sacrocolpopexy preserves function but is a longer abdominal operation with mesh risks, anterior repair alone leaves apical prolapse, and muscle training does not reverse stage 4 prolapse.

items.stem: A 29-year-old G1P0 woman at 34 weeks has intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy treated with ursodeoxycholic acid. Her total bile acid level is 112 micromol/L, and fetal testing is reassuring. Which is the best recommendation for delivery?
options: Deliver at 39 0/7 weeks, since testing is reassuring
Deliver at 38 0/7 weeks, as for lower bile acid levels
Offer delivery at 36 0/7 weeks
Continue to 40 0/7 weeks with weekly testing
items.explanation: Stillbirth risk in intrahepatic cholestasis rises with bile acid concentration, especially at 100 micromol/L or more, so delivery is planned earlier, at 36 0/7 weeks, for such values, while lower levels allow delivery between 36 and 39 weeks. Ursodeoxycholic acid relieves itching but has not been shown to remove the stillbirth risk, and reassuring testing does not predict sudden fetal death. Waiting to 38 or 39 weeks, or to term, accepts that risk.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman has had bacterial vaginosis three times in the past year, each confirmed by Amsel criteria and cured with oral metronidazole. She is not pregnant. Which plan best reduces further recurrence?
options: Metronidazole 0.75 percent vaginal gel twice weekly for 4 to 6 months
Routine treatment of her male partner with oral metronidazole
Repeated single-dose fluconazole
Daily douching with an acidic solution
items.explanation: After three or more recurrences, suppressive therapy with metronidazole vaginal gel twice weekly for 4 to 6 months lowers relapse, although recurrence often follows when it stops, so she should be counseled about this. Treating male partners has not reduced recurrence. Fluconazole treats yeast, not bacterial vaginosis, and douching disturbs the lactobacilli that keep the vaginal flora protective, which increases recurrence.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman with epilepsy has been seizure free for two years on lamotrigine monotherapy and is now 8 weeks pregnant. What is the best plan for her medication?
options: Stop it until the second trimester begins
Continue it, check serum levels, and adjust the dose as pregnancy advances
Halve the dose to limit fetal exposure
Change to valproate for stronger seizure control
items.explanation: Lamotrigine is among the safer antiseizure drugs, and seizures themselves endanger mother and fetus, so therapy continues at the lowest effective dose. Its clearance rises substantially in pregnancy, which can lower levels and allow breakthrough seizures, so levels are checked and the dose adjusted, then reduced again after delivery. Stopping or halving the drug invites seizures, and valproate carries the highest rates of neural tube defects and neurodevelopmental harm.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman has had amenorrhea for 8 months with hot flashes. FSH is 62 mIU/mL on two occasions a month apart and karyotype is 46,XX. She has no contraindications to hormone therapy and has a normal bone density scan. What is the best management?
options: Short-term hormone therapy limited to five years
Calcium and vitamin D only, with no hormone therapy
Ovulation induction with clomiphene for pregnancy
Hormone therapy until at least the usual age of natural menopause
items.explanation: Elevated FSH on two occasions with amenorrhea before age 40 establishes primary ovarian insufficiency, and estrogen deficiency raises the risk of osteoporosis, heart disease, and cognitive decline. Replacement is advised until about age 51, when risks and benefits are reassessed, and is not subject to the cautions that apply to older women. Supplements alone are insufficient, and clomiphene is ineffective with exhausted follicles.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman at 37 weeks has had one prior cesarean through a vertical incision that extended into the contractile fundus. She asks about a trial of labor. What is the best counseling?
options: Offer labor with a transcervical balloon for ripening
Labor is not advised; recommend a planned repeat cesarean
Offer labor with misoprostol for ripening
Offer labor with epidural analgesia and continuous monitoring
items.explanation: A prior classical or other vertical uterine incision extending into the contractile fundus carries a substantially higher risk of uterine rupture in labor, so a trial of labor is contraindicated and a planned repeat cesarean before labor begins is recommended. Mechanical ripening, prostaglandins, or close monitoring do not remove the risk of rupture through a fundal scar. A low transverse scar, by contrast, permits a trial of labor.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman has a 6 cm unilocular, thin-walled, anechoic ovarian cyst with posterior enhancement found incidentally on ultrasonography. She has no symptoms, and the cyst has no solid components or internal flow. What is the best management?
options: Follow with repeat pelvic ultrasonography
Laparoscopic cystectomy now
CA-125 measurement followed by oophorectomy
Oral contraceptive pills to make the cyst regress
items.explanation: A simple cyst in a premenopausal woman carries a very low risk of malignancy. Those up to about 5 cm need no follow-up, and larger ones are followed with repeat imaging, with further evaluation reserved for cysts above roughly 7 cm or a change in features. Surgery now is unnecessary, tumor markers are unreliable in premenopausal women, and oral contraceptives do not hasten resolution of functional cysts.

items.stem: A 28-year-old G1P0 woman at 34 weeks is admitted in preterm labor with progressive cervical change. Her group B streptococcus status is unknown, and she has no drug allergies. What is the best management regarding prophylaxis?
options: Await a culture result before giving any antibiotic
Oral amoxicillin for 5 days, then discharge
Ampicillin and gentamicin for presumed intraamniotic infection
Intravenous penicillin G now, continued until delivery
items.explanation: Preterm labor with unknown group B streptococcus status is an indication for intrapartum prophylaxis, because preterm delivery raises the risk of neonatal sepsis. Intravenous penicillin G is started on admission and continued until delivery, and it is stopped if labor ceases and cultures are negative. Waiting for results delays protection, an oral course does not give intrapartum levels, and ampicillin with gentamicin treats suspected infection, which she does not have.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman three months after molar evacuation has a rising hCG of 62,000 mIU/mL and multiple lung nodules on chest imaging. Her FIGO prognostic score is 9. Which is the best treatment?
options: Single-agent methotrexate
Repeat suction curettage
Multiagent chemotherapy such as EMA-CO
Hysterectomy alone
items.explanation: A FIGO score of 7 or more defines high-risk gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, which is treated with multiagent chemotherapy such as etoposide, methotrexate, dactinomycin, cyclophosphamide, and vincristine, because single agents fail in this group. Single-agent methotrexate or dactinomycin is for scores of 6 or less. Repeat curettage rarely helps, and hysterectomy alone does not treat metastases.

items.stem: A 28-year-old G2P1 woman at 35 weeks has leaking of clear fluid for six hours, with pooling and ferning confirmed. She has no contractions or fever, the tracing is reassuring, and her group B streptococcus status is unknown. Which is the best management?
options: Admit for expectant care until 37 weeks with corticosteroids
Proceed to delivery with group B streptococcus prophylaxis
Discharge for outpatient expectant care with weekly visits
Place an emergency cerclage to seal the membranes
items.explanation: At 34 0/7 weeks or later, ruptured membranes are managed with delivery, because the risks of infection, abruption, and cord prolapse outweigh the small benefit of further maturation. Group B streptococcus prophylaxis is given when status is unknown. Expectant care to 37 weeks belongs to earlier gestations, outpatient care is unsafe after rupture, and a cerclage is contraindicated once the membranes have ruptured.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman has fatigue, weight gain, amenorrhea, and milky nipple discharge. Pregnancy test is negative, TSH is 28 mIU/L with a low free thyroxine, and prolactin is 60 ng/mL. Which is the best treatment?
options: Cabergoline
Transsphenoidal surgery
Combined hormonal contraception
Levothyroxine
items.explanation: Primary hypothyroidism raises thyrotropin-releasing hormone, which stimulates prolactin release and causes amenorrhea and galactorrhea. Replacing thyroid hormone corrects both the thyroid state and the prolactin level, usually restoring menses, which is why TSH is checked in every woman with galactorrhea. A dopamine agonist or pituitary surgery treats a prolactinoma, which is not the cause here, and contraception would mask the amenorrhea without treating its cause.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman who is breastfeeding her 4-week-old infant has had mastitis for five days despite cephalexin. She now has a fever of 38.7 degrees Celsius and a tender, fluctuant 4 cm mass in the left breast. What is the best management?
options: Ultrasound-guided drainage, antibiotics, and continued breastfeeding
Stop breastfeeding and give oral antibiotics for ten days
Warm compresses with reassessment in two weeks
Cold packs and a higher dose of the same antibiotic
items.explanation: A fluctuant mass that follows mastitis is a breast abscess, which needs drainage by ultrasound-guided needle aspiration or incision, together with antibiotics active against Staphylococcus aureus and continued milk removal from the breast. Breastfeeding is safe and speeds recovery. Antibiotics alone will not resolve a collection, and weaning or compresses without drainage let it enlarge. Cultures guide therapy when methicillin-resistant organisms are suspected.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman has progressively heavy, painful periods. The uterus is globular, tender, and mildly enlarged. Endometrial biopsy is benign and ultrasonography shows myometrial cysts with an indistinct endometrial-myometrial junction. She wants to retain her uterus and does not want pregnancy. Which is the best initial treatment?
options: Uterine artery embolization
Hysteroscopic polypectomy
A levonorgestrel intrauterine system
Ulipristal for emergency contraception
items.explanation: A globular tender uterus with myometrial cysts is characteristic of adenomyosis, for which a levonorgestrel intrauterine system reduces bleeding and pain and is a reasonable first-line therapy when fertility is not desired and the patient prefers conservation. Hysterectomy is definitive but not mandatory. Embolization is a later option, polypectomy treats focal lesions, and emergency contraception has no therapeutic role.

items.stem: A 30-year-old primipara at her 6-week visit scores 16 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, with low mood, poor concentration, and guilt for four weeks. She denies thoughts of self-harm or of harming the baby and is breastfeeding. What is the best management?
options: Reassure her that postpartum blues will resolve
Start sertraline and refer for psychotherapy
Prescribe a benzodiazepine for sleep and anxiety
Admit her involuntarily for psychiatric care
items.explanation: A high screening score with symptoms lasting beyond two weeks indicates postpartum depression rather than blues. Treatment is psychotherapy, an antidepressant, or both, and sertraline is compatible with breastfeeding. Reassurance misses a treatable disorder lasting weeks, benzodiazepines do not treat depression and add dependence risk, and involuntary admission is for psychosis or imminent danger, which she does not show. Suicide risk is reassessed at every visit.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman has a unifocal 1 cm white plaque on the left labium minus. Biopsy shows high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (vulvar HSIL, usual type) with no invasion, and she is HPV 16 positive. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Radical vulvectomy with bilateral inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy
Repeat biopsy and observation for one year
Wide local excision with a negative margin
Simple vulvectomy with reconstruction
items.explanation: Usual-type vulvar HSIL is a premalignant lesion with a real progression risk, so treatment is indicated. A unifocal lesion is best managed by wide local excision, which confirms the absence of occult invasion on the whole specimen. Radical vulvectomy with node dissection and simple vulvectomy are overtreatment for a noninvasive lesion, and observation leaves a persistent HPV-driven lesion in place.

items.stem: A 25-year-old G1P0 woman at 7 weeks has nausea and vomiting three to four times daily. She has no weight loss, ketonuria, or dehydration and wants treatment. Which is the first-line medication?
options: Doxylamine with pyridoxine
Intravenous dextrose with thiamine
Oral ondansetron as the first agent
Intravenous methylprednisolone
items.explanation: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy without dehydration or weight loss is treated first with dietary measures and the combination of doxylamine and pyridoxine, which has the longest safety record. Intravenous fluids are for dehydration or ketosis, ondansetron is a second-line addition, and corticosteroids are reserved for refractory hyperemesis because of limited safety data early in pregnancy.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman reports burning and pain with intercourse. Examination shows pale, thin vaginal mucosa without rugae. Vaginal pH is 6.5, and microscopy shows parabasal cells with few lactobacilli. Which is the best treatment?
options: Oral metronidazole
Topical clobetasol
Systemic testosterone
Low-dose vaginal estrogen
items.explanation: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause causes dyspareunia, an elevated pH, and parabasal cells from estrogen deficiency, and low-dose vaginal estrogen is the most effective therapy with minimal systemic absorption. Metronidazole treats infections such as bacterial vaginosis, clobetasol treats lichen sclerosus, and testosterone is not approved for this indication, does not restore the epithelium, and carries its own adverse effects.
